draft.title: Pleas and charge negotiation
card: A plea is the accused's answer to a charge. A guilty plea admits the offence, so there is no trial on guilt and the court moves to sentencing. A not guilty plea sends the case to trial, where the prosecution must prove it.

In charge negotiation, the prosecution and defence talk before the trial. The accused agrees to plead guilty to a lesser charge or to fewer charges. In return, the prosecution drops the other charges.
It saves time and cost, and the court does not need a full trial. Witnesses, including victims, may not have to give evidence.
It can seem unfair to victims. The accused may be convicted of a lesser offence than the crime the victim believes was committed, and the sentence may be lighter.
draft.remember: Charge negotiation trades a guilty plea for a lesser or fewer charges, which saves time but can feel unfair to victims.

a.q: What does an accused person agree to do in charge negotiation?
opts: Plead guilty to a lesser charge or fewer charges
Plead not guilty to every charge laid against them
Skip the plea and ask the judge to dismiss the case
Plead guilty to all charges in return for a jury trial
a.why: In charge negotiation the accused gives a guilty plea, and in return the prosecution drops some charges or accepts a lesser one. Pleading not guilty to every charge is wrong because that sends the case to trial, so nothing is negotiated.
a.clue: The accused gives something up and gets something back.

b.q: Dev is charged with two offences. He agrees to plead guilty to one, and the prosecution drops the other. The victim, Sam, says this is unfair. What is the most likely reason for Sam's view?
opts: Dev may be convicted of less than Sam thinks he did
Dev will have to face a full jury trial on both charges
Sam will have to give evidence for several days in court
Dev's guilty plea means the court cannot sentence him
b.why: Charge negotiation can leave an accused convicted of fewer or lesser offences, so a victim may feel the outcome does not match what happened. The option about a full trial is wrong because a guilty plea avoids a trial on guilt.
b.clue: Think about what the dropped charge means for the outcome.

a.best: Plead guilty to a lesser charge or fewer charges

b.best: Dev may be convicted of less than Sam thinks he did

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may'). The three wrong options use flat certainties ('cannot', 'will have to'), so a test-wise student could pick the answer without knowing the idea. Give the distractors similar hedges, or drop 'may' from the right option.
